facts.title: Named for a Living Legend
facts.text: Seaborgium is named after the American nuclear chemist Glenn T. Seaborg, who co-discovered plutonium and nine other elements. It was the first element ever officially named after a person who was still alive at the time of naming in 1997. Seaborg reportedly said it was the greatest honor of his life, even greater than his 1951 Nobel Prize.

facts.title: Born in a Berkeley Lab
facts.text: Seaborgium was first created in 1974 by a team led by Albert Ghiorso and Kenneth Hulet at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. They bombarded a target of californium-249 with oxygen-18 ions to produce a few atoms of seaborgium-263. A competing Soviet team in Dubna had reported related work, sparking a years-long naming dispute known as the 'Transfermium Wars.'

facts.title: A Fleeting Existence
facts.text: Seaborgium is intensely radioactive and exists only for the briefest moments before decaying. Its longest-lived known isotope, seaborgium-269, has a half-life of roughly two to three minutes, while many isotopes vanish in fractions of a second. Because of this, every seaborgium atom ever made has long since decayed away.

facts.title: Counted Atom by Atom
facts.text: Scientists have never assembled a visible, weighable sample of seaborgium; it has only been produced a handful of atoms at a time. Researchers must study its chemistry using single atoms before they decay, a field called 'atom-at-a-time' chemistry. This makes seaborgium one of the most experimentally challenging substances to investigate.

facts.title: It Behaves Like Tungsten
facts.text: Despite being a synthetic superheavy element, seaborgium sits in group 6 of the periodic table, directly below chromium, molybdenum, and tungsten. Pioneering experiments in the late 1990s confirmed it forms volatile oxide and oxychloride compounds much like tungsten does. This was a triumph for the periodic law, showing chemical patterns hold even for element 106.

facts.title: A Carbonyl Surprise
facts.text: In 2014, an international team at the GSI laboratory in Germany synthesized seaborgium hexacarbonyl, Sg(CO)6, the first complex of a superheavy element with carbon monoxide. This showed seaborgium can form a stable metal-carbonyl bond just like its lighter cousins. It was a landmark in proving that classic coordination chemistry extends to the heaviest known metals.

facts.title: Made One Nucleus at a Time
facts.text: Creating seaborgium requires slamming heavy ions into a target inside a particle accelerator at enormous energies. Even with a beam delivering trillions of projectiles per second, only a few atoms might be produced over days of running. The product atoms are then whisked away by gas-filled separators to be detected before they decay.

facts.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Electrons
facts.text: In superheavy atoms like seaborgium, electrons near the nucleus move at a sizable fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity noticeably alters their orbitals. These relativistic effects can subtly shift bonding and stability compared with lighter group-6 metals. Studying seaborgium tests how well our quantum models hold up at the extreme edge of the periodic table.

facts.title: No Place in Nature
facts.text: Seaborgium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth or, as far as we know, in stars or supernovae in any lasting amount. It is entirely human-made, existing only inside laboratories with powerful accelerators. With no natural source and no stable isotope, it has zero biological role and no presence in living organisms.

facts.title: Purely a Research Element
facts.text: Seaborgium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications and almost certainly never will, because it cannot be made in useful quantities and decays too fast. Its entire value is scientific: it lets chemists probe the limits of the periodic table and the behavior of matter at extreme atomic numbers. In that sense, seaborgium is a tool for understanding nature rather than a material to be used.
